evidence_span.text:
WITH text_input(id, text) AS (
         VALUES
             (1, 'The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog'),
             (2, 'The quick and the lazy'),
             (3, 'The quick brown fox jumps over the dog')
     ),
     text_ngrams(id, ngrams) AS (
         SELECT id,
                transform(
                  ngrams(
                    split(text, ' '),
                    4
                  ),
                  token -> array_join(token, ' ')
                )
         FROM text_input
     ),
     minhash_digest(id, digest) AS (
         SELECT id,
                (SELECT make_set_digest(v) FROM unnest(ngrams) u(v))
         FROM text_ngrams
     ),
     setdigest_side_by_side(id1, digest1, id2, digest2) AS (
         SELECT m1.id as id1,
                m1.digest as digest1,
                m2.id as id2,
                m2.digest as digest2
         FROM (SELECT id, digest FROM minhash_digest) m1
         JOIN (SELECT id, digest FROM minhash_digest) m2
           ON m1.id != m2.id AND m1.id < m2.id
     )
SELECT id1,
       id2,
       intersection_cardinality(digest1, digest2) AS intersection_cardinality,
       jaccard_index(digest1, digest2)            AS jaccard_index
FROM setdigest_side_by_side
ORDER BY id1, id2;

evidence_span.text: json_exists #

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators #

evidence_span.text: The json_exists function determines whether a JSON value satisfies a JSON path specification.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_exists #

evidence_span.text:
JSON_EXISTS(
    json_input [ FORMAT JSON [ ENCODING { UTF8 | UTF16 | UTF32 } ] ],
    json_path
    [ PASSING json_argument [, ...] ]
    [ { TRUE | FALSE | UNKNOWN | ERROR } ON ERROR ]
    )

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_exists #

evidence_span.text: The json_path is evaluated using the json_input as the context variable ( $ ), and the passed arguments as the named variables ( $variable_name ). The returned value is true if the path returns a non-empty sequence, and false if the path returns an empty sequence. If an error occurs, the returned value depends on the ON ERROR clause. The default value returned ON ERROR is FALSE . The ON ERROR clause is applied for the following kinds of errors:

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_exists #

evidence_span.text: Input conversion errors, such as malformed JSON

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_exists #

evidence_span.text: JSON path evaluation errors, e.g. division by zero

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_exists #

evidence_span.text: json_input is a JSON value, a character string, or a binary string. A string should contain a single JSON item; for a binary string, you can specify encoding.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_exists #

evidence_span.text: json_path is a string literal, containing the path mode specification, and the path expression, following the syntax rules described in JSON path syntax and semantics .

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_exists #

evidence_span.text:
'strict ($.price + $.tax)?(@ > 99.9)'
'lax $[0 to 1].floor()?(@ > 10)'

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_exists #

evidence_span.text: In the PASSING clause you can pass arbitrary expressions to be used by the path expression.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_exists #

evidence_span.text:
PASSING orders.totalprice AS O_PRICE,
        orders.tax % 10 AS O_TAX

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_exists #

evidence_span.text: The passed parameters can be referenced in the path expression by named variables, prefixed with $ .

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_exists #

evidence_span.text: 'lax $?(@.price > $O_PRICE || @.tax > $O_TAX)'

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_exists #

evidence_span.text: Additionally to SQL values, you can pass JSON values, specifying the format and optional encoding:

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_exists #

evidence_span.text:
PASSING orders.json_desc FORMAT JSON AS o_desc,
        orders.binary_record FORMAT JSON ENCODING UTF16 AS o_rec

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_exists #

evidence_span.text: Note that the JSON path language is case-sensitive, while the unquoted SQL identifiers are upper-cased. Therefore, it is recommended to use quoted identifiers in the PASSING clause:

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_exists #

evidence_span.text:
'lax $.keyvalue()?(@.name == $KeyName).value' PASSING nation.name AS KeyName --> ERROR; no passed value found
'lax $.keyvalue()?(@.name == $KeyName).value' PASSING nation.name AS "KeyName" --> correct

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_exists #

evidence_span.text: Examples #

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_exists #

evidence_span.text: Let customers be a table containing two columns: id:bigint , description:varchar .

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_exists # / Examples #

evidence_span.text: json_value #

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators #

evidence_span.text: The json_value function extracts a scalar SQL value from a JSON value.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_value #

evidence_span.text:
JSON_VALUE(
    json_input [ FORMAT JSON [ ENCODING { UTF8 | UTF16 | UTF32 } ] ],
    json_path
    [ PASSING json_argument [, ...] ]
    [ RETURNING type ]
    [ { ERROR | NULL | DEFAULT expression } ON EMPTY ]
    [ { ERROR | NULL | DEFAULT expression } ON ERROR ]
    )

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_value #

evidence_span.text: The json_path is evaluated using the json_input as the context variable ( $ ), and the passed arguments as the named variables ( $variable_name ).

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_value #

evidence_span.text: The returned value is the SQL scalar returned by the path. By default, it is converted to string ( varchar ). In the RETURNING clause, you can specify other desired type: a character string type, numeric, boolean or datetime type.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_value #

evidence_span.text: json_input is a JSON value, a character string, or a binary string. A string should contain a single JSON item; for a binary string, you can specify encoding.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_value #

evidence_span.text: json_path is a string literal, containing the path mode specification, and the path expression, following the syntax rules described in JSON path syntax and semantics .

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_value #

evidence_span.text:
'strict $.price + $tax'
'lax $[last].abs().floor()'

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_value #

evidence_span.text: In the PASSING clause you can pass arbitrary expressions to be used by the path expression.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_value #

evidence_span.text: PASSING orders.tax AS O_TAX

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_value #

evidence_span.text: The passed parameters can be referenced in the path expression by named variables, prefixed with $ .

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_value #

evidence_span.text: 'strict $[last].price + $O_TAX'

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_value #

evidence_span.text: Additionally to SQL values, you can pass JSON values, specifying the format and optional encoding:

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_value #

evidence_span.text:
PASSING orders.json_desc FORMAT JSON AS o_desc,
        orders.binary_record FORMAT JSON ENCODING UTF16 AS o_rec

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_value #

evidence_span.text: Note that the JSON path language is case-sensitive, while the unquoted SQL identifiers are upper-cased. Therefore, it is recommended to use quoted identifiers in the PASSING clause:

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_value #

evidence_span.text:
'lax $.keyvalue()?(@.name == $KeyName).value' PASSING nation.name AS KeyName --> ERROR; no passed value found
'lax $.keyvalue()?(@.name == $KeyName).value' PASSING nation.name AS "KeyName" --> correct

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_value #

evidence_span.text: If the path returns an empty sequence, the ON EMPTY clause is applied. The default value returned ON EMPTY is NULL . You can also specify the default value:

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_value #

evidence_span.text: DEFAULT -1 ON EMPTY

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_value #

evidence_span.text: If an error occurs, the returned value depends on the ON ERROR clause. The default value returned ON ERROR is NULL . One example of error is multiple items returned by the path. Other errors caught and handled according to the ON ERROR clause are:

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_value #

evidence_span.text: Input conversion errors, such as malformed JSON

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_value #

evidence_span.text: JSON path evaluation errors, e.g. division by zero

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_value #

evidence_span.text: Returned scalar not convertible to the desired type

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_value #

evidence_span.text: The DEFAULT expression in ON EMPTY and ON ERROR is only evaluated when the corresponding branch is taken. If evaluation of the ON EMPTY default itself raises a data exception, the failure cascades to the ON ERROR clause. Subqueries are not supported in DEFAULT expressions.

evidence_span.text: json_table #

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators #

evidence_span.text: The json_table clause extracts a table from a JSON value. Use this clause to transform JSON data into a relational format, making it easier to query and analyze. Use json_table in the FROM clause of a SELECT statement to create a table from JSON data.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_table #

evidence_span.text:
JSON_TABLE(
    json_input,
    json_path [ AS path_name ]
    [ PASSING value AS parameter_name [, ...] ]
    COLUMNS (
        column_definition [, ...] )
    [ PLAN ( json_table_specific_plan )
      | PLAN DEFAULT ( json_table_default_plan ) ]
    [ { ERROR | EMPTY } ON ERROR ]
)

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_table #

evidence_span.text: The COLUMNS clause supports the following column_definition arguments:

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_table #

evidence_span.text:
column_name FOR ORDINALITY
| column_name type
    [ FORMAT JSON [ ENCODING { UTF8 | UTF16 | UTF32 } ] ]
    [ PATH json_path ]
    [ { WITHOUT | WITH { CONDITIONAL | UNCONDITIONAL } } [ ARRAY ] WRAPPER ]
    [ { KEEP | OMIT } QUOTES [ ON SCALAR STRING ] ]
    [ { ERROR | NULL | EMPTY { [ARRAY] | OBJECT } | DEFAULT expression } ON EMPTY ]
    [ { ERROR | NULL | DEFAULT expression } ON ERROR ]
| NESTED [ PATH ] json_path [ AS path_name ] COLUMNS ( column_definition [, ...] )

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_table #

evidence_span.text: json_input is a JSON value, a character string, or a binary string. A string must contain a single JSON item.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_table #

evidence_span.text: json_path is a string literal containing the path mode specification and the path expression. It follows the syntax rules described in JSON path syntax and semantics .

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_table #

evidence_span.text:
'strict ($.price + $.tax)?(@ > 99.9)'
'lax $[0 to 1].floor()?(@ > 10)'

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_table #

evidence_span.text: In the PASSING clause, pass values as named parameters that the json_path expression can reference.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_table #

evidence_span.text:
PASSING orders.totalprice AS o_price,
        orders.tax % 10 AS o_tax

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_table #

evidence_span.text: Use named parameters to reference the values in the path expression. Prefix named parameters with $ .

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_table #

evidence_span.text: 'lax $?(@.price > $o_price || @.tax > $o_tax)'

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_table #

evidence_span.text: You can also pass JSON values in the PASSING clause. Use FORMAT JSON to specify the format and ENCODING to specify the encoding:

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_table #

evidence_span.text:
PASSING orders.json_desc FORMAT JSON AS o_desc,
        orders.binary_record FORMAT JSON ENCODING UTF16 AS o_rec

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_table #

evidence_span.text: The json_path value is case-sensitive. The SQL identifiers are uppercase. Use quoted identifiers in the PASSING clause:

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_table #

evidence_span.text:
'lax $.keyvalue()?(@.name == $KeyName).value' PASSING nation.name AS KeyName --> ERROR; no passed value found
'lax $.keyvalue()?(@.name == $KeyName).value' PASSING nation.name AS "KeyName" --> correct

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_table #

evidence_span.text: The PLAN clause specifies how to join columns from different paths. Use OUTER or INNER to define how to join parent paths with their child paths. Use CROSS or UNION to join siblings.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_table #

evidence_span.text: COLUMNS defines the schema of your table. Each column_definition specifies how to extract and format your json_input value into a relational column.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_table #

evidence_span.text: PLAN is an optional clause to control how to process and join nested JSON data.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_table #

evidence_span.text: ON ERROR specifies how to handle processing errors. ERROR ON ERROR throws an error. EMPTY ON ERROR returns an empty result set.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_table #

evidence_span.text: For each value column with DEFAULT in its ON EMPTY or ON ERROR clause, the default expression is only evaluated when the corresponding branch is taken, and if the ON EMPTY default itself raises a data exception, the failure cascades to the ON ERROR clause. Subqueries are not supported in json_table DEFAULT expressions.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_table #

evidence_span.text: column_name specifies a column name.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_table #

evidence_span.text: FOR ORDINALITY adds a row number column to the output table, starting at 1 . Specify the column name in the column definition:

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_table #

evidence_span.text: row_num FOR ORDINALITY

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_table #

evidence_span.text: NESTED PATH extracts data from nested levels of a json_input value. Each NESTED PATH clause can contain column_definition values.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_table #

evidence_span.text: The json_table function returns a result set that you can use like any other table in your queries. You can join the result set with other tables or combine multiple arrays from your JSON data.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_table #

evidence_span.text: You can also process nested JSON objects without parsing the data multiple times.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_table #

evidence_span.text: Use json_table as a lateral join to process JSON data from another table.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_table #

evidence_span.text: Examples #

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_table #

field_reviews.raw_text: The IS [NOT] TRUE , IS [NOT] FALSE , and IS [NOT] UNKNOWN operators test the three-valued result of a boolean expression. Unlike a direct comparison against TRUE or FALSE , these operators always return a non-null boolean, treating a NULL (unknown) operand as a known value. IS UNKNOWN is equivalent to IS NULL on a boolean operand:
SELECT ( 1 > 0 ) IS TRUE ; -- true SELECT ( 1 > 2 ) IS FALSE ; -- true SELECT ( NULL > 0 ) IS UNKNOWN ; -- true SELECT ( NULL > 0 ) IS NOT TRUE ; -- true

evidence_span.text:
WITH text_input(id, text) AS (
         VALUES
             (1, 'The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog'),
             (2, 'The quick and the lazy'),
             (3, 'The quick brown fox jumps over the dog')
     ),
     text_ngrams(id, ngrams) AS (
         SELECT id,
                transform(
                  ngrams(
                    split(text, ' '),
                    4
                  ),
                  token -> array_join(token, ' ')
                )
         FROM text_input
     ),
     minhash_digest(id, digest) AS (
         SELECT id,
                (SELECT make_set_digest(v) FROM unnest(ngrams) u(v))
         FROM text_ngrams
     ),
     setdigest_side_by_side(id1, digest1, id2, digest2) AS (
         SELECT m1.id as id1,
                m1.digest as digest1,
                m2.id as id2,
                m2.digest as digest2
         FROM (SELECT id, digest FROM minhash_digest) m1
         JOIN (SELECT id, digest FROM minhash_digest) m2
           ON m1.id != m2.id AND m1.id < m2.id
     )
SELECT id1,
       id2,
       intersection_cardinality(digest1, digest2) AS intersection_cardinality,
       jaccard_index(digest1, digest2)            AS jaccard_index
FROM setdigest_side_by_side
ORDER BY id1, id2;

evidence_span.text: Uniqueness test: UNIQUE #
The UNIQUE predicate tests whether a subquery contains duplicate rows. It returns true when no two rows of the subquery are equal, and false otherwise:

supporting_evidence.section_heading: Comparison functions and operators # / Uniqueness test: UNIQUE #

evidence_span.text: UNIQUE ( subquery )

supporting_evidence.section_heading: Comparison functions and operators # / Uniqueness test: UNIQUE #

evidence_span.text:
SELECT UNIQUE (VALUES 1, 2, 3); -- true

SELECT UNIQUE (VALUES 1, 1, 2); -- false

supporting_evidence.section_heading: Comparison functions and operators # / Uniqueness test: UNIQUE #

evidence_span.text: A row that contains a NULL in any column is never counted as a duplicate, not even of an identical row. Only rows whose columns are all non-null can form a duplicate pair:

supporting_evidence.section_heading: Comparison functions and operators # / Uniqueness test: UNIQUE #

evidence_span.text:
-- the two rows are identical, but each contains a NULL, so they are not duplicates
SELECT UNIQUE (VALUES (CAST(NULL AS integer), 'a'), (CAST(NULL AS integer), 'a')); -- true

-- the (1, 'b') pair is a duplicate; the NULL row is irrelevant
SELECT UNIQUE (VALUES (CAST(NULL AS integer), 'a'), (1, 'b'), (1, 'b')); -- false

supporting_evidence.section_heading: Comparison functions and operators # / Uniqueness test: UNIQUE #

evidence_span.text: As a result, an empty subquery and a subquery in which every row contains a NULL both satisfy UNIQUE :

supporting_evidence.section_heading: Comparison functions and operators # / Uniqueness test: UNIQUE #

evidence_span.text: SELECT UNIQUE (SELECT 1 WHERE false); -- true

supporting_evidence.section_heading: Comparison functions and operators # / Uniqueness test: UNIQUE #

evidence_span.text: Use NOT to test for the presence of a duplicate:

supporting_evidence.section_heading: Comparison functions and operators # / Uniqueness test: UNIQUE #

evidence_span.text: SELECT NOT UNIQUE (VALUES 1, 1); -- true

supporting_evidence.section_heading: Comparison functions and operators # / Uniqueness test: UNIQUE #

evidence_span.text: Note

supporting_evidence.section_heading: Comparison functions and operators # / Uniqueness test: UNIQUE #

evidence_span.text: The subquery of a UNIQUE predicate cannot be correlated with the enclosing query.

evidence_span.text: Returns the JSON text serialized from the input JSON value. This is inverse function to json_parse() . SELECT json_format ( JSON '[1, 2, 3]' ); -- '[1,2,3]' SELECT json_format ( JSON '"a"' ); -- '"a"' Note json_format() and CAST(json AS VARCHAR) have completely different semantics. json_format() serializes the input JSON value to JSON text conforming to RFC 7159 . The JSON value can be a JSON object, a JSON array, a JSON string, a JSON number, true , false or null . SELECT json_format ( JSON '{"a": 1, "b": 2}' ); -- '{"a":1,"b":2}' SELECT json_format ( JSON '[1, 2, 3]' ); -- '[1,2,3]' SELECT json_format ( JSON '"abc"' ); -- '"abc"' SELECT json_format ( JSON '42' ); -- '42' SELECT json_format ( JSON 'true' ); -- 'true' SELECT json_format ( JSON 'null' ); -- 'null' CAST(json AS VARCHAR) casts the JSON value to the corresponding SQL VARCHAR value. For JSON string, JSON number, true , false or null , the cast behavior is same as the corresponding SQL type. JSON object and JSON array cannot be cast to VARCHAR. SELECT CAST ( JSON '{"a": 1, "b": 2}' AS VARCHAR ); -- ERROR! SELECT CAST ( JSON '[1, 2, 3]' AS VARCHAR ); -- ERROR! SELECT CAST ( JSON '"abc"' AS VARCHAR ); -- 'abc' (the double quote is gone) SELECT CAST ( JSON '42' AS VARCHAR ); -- '42' SELECT CAST ( JSON 'true' AS VARCHAR ); -- 'true' SELECT CAST ( JSON 'null' AS VARCHAR ); -- NULL

evidence_span.text: Renders a single line in an ANSI bar chart of the specified width . The parameter x is a double value between 0 and 1. Values of x that fall outside the range [0, 1] will be truncated to either a 0 or a 1 value. The low_color and high_color capture the color to use for either end of the horizontal bar chart. For example, if x is 0.5, width is 80, low_color is 0xFF0000, and high_color is 0x00FF00 this function will return a 40 character bar that varies from red (0xFF0000) and yellow (0xFFFF00) and the remainder of the 80 character bar will be padded with spaces.

field_reviews.raw_text: The ALL , ANY and SOME quantifiers can be used together with comparison operators in the following way:
SELECT 'hello' = ANY ( VALUES 'hello' , 'world' ); -- true SELECT 21 < ALL ( VALUES 19 , 20 , 21 ); -- false SELECT 42 >= SOME ( SELECT 41 UNION ALL SELECT 42 UNION ALL SELECT 43 ); -- true
Following are the meanings of some quantifier and comparison operator combinations:
Evaluates to true when A is equal to all values.
Evaluates to true when A doesn’t match any value.
Evaluates to true when A is smaller than the smallest value.
Evaluates to true when A is equal to any of the values. This form is equivalent to A IN (...) .
Evaluates to true when A doesn’t match one or more values.
Evaluates to true when A is smaller than the biggest value.
ANY and SOME have the same meaning and can be used interchangeably.

field_reviews.raw_text: The IS [NOT] TRUE , IS [NOT] FALSE , and IS [NOT] UNKNOWN operators test the three-valued result of a boolean expression. Unlike a direct comparison against TRUE or FALSE , these operators always return a non-null boolean, treating a NULL (unknown) operand as a known value. IS UNKNOWN is equivalent to IS NULL on a boolean operand:
SELECT ( 1 > 0 ) IS TRUE ; -- true SELECT ( 1 > 2 ) IS FALSE ; -- true SELECT ( NULL > 0 ) IS UNKNOWN ; -- true SELECT ( NULL > 0 ) IS NOT TRUE ; -- true
The following truth table demonstrates the handling of each truth value:

evidence_span.text: IS TRUE, IS FALSE, and IS UNKNOWN #

The IS [NOT] TRUE , IS [NOT] FALSE , and IS [NOT] UNKNOWN operators test the three-valued result of a boolean expression. Unlike a direct comparison against TRUE or FALSE , these operators always return a non-null boolean, treating a NULL (unknown) operand as a known value. IS UNKNOWN is equivalent to IS NULL on a boolean operand:

supporting_evidence.section_heading: Comparison functions and operators # / IS TRUE, IS FALSE, and IS UNKNOWN #

evidence_span.text:
SELECT (1 > 0) IS TRUE; -- true

SELECT (1 > 2) IS FALSE; -- true

SELECT (NULL > 0) IS UNKNOWN; -- true

SELECT (NULL > 0) IS NOT TRUE; -- true

evidence_span.text:
SELECT reduce(ARRAY[], 0,
              (s, x) -> s + x,
              s -> s);
-- 0

SELECT reduce(ARRAY[5, 20, 50], 0,
              (s, x) -> s + x,
              s -> s);
-- 75

SELECT reduce(ARRAY[5, 20, NULL, 50], 0,
              (s, x) -> s + x,
              s -> s);
-- NULL

SELECT reduce(ARRAY[5, 20, NULL, 50], 0,
              (s, x) -> s + coalesce(x, 0),
              s -> s);
-- 75

SELECT reduce(ARRAY[5, 20, NULL, 50], 0,
              (s, x) -> IF(x IS NULL, s, s + x),
              s -> s);
-- 75

SELECT reduce(ARRAY[2147483647, 1], BIGINT '0',
              (s, x) -> s + x,
              s -> s);
-- 2147483648

-- calculates arithmetic average
SELECT reduce(ARRAY[5, 6, 10, 20],
              CAST(ROW(0.0, 0) AS ROW(sum DOUBLE, count INTEGER)),
              (s, x) -> CAST(ROW(x + s.sum, s.count + 1) AS
                             ROW(sum DOUBLE, count INTEGER)),
              s -> IF(s.count = 0, NULL, s.sum / s.count));
-- 10.25

evidence_span.text: Returns the logical right shifted value of value . Shifting 8 (binary: 1000 ) by three bits results in 1 (binary: 001 ): SELECT bitwise_right_shift ( 8 , 3 ); -- 1 Shifting 9 (binary: 1001 ) by one bit results in 4 (binary: 100 ): SELECT bitwise_right_shift ( 9 , 1 ); -- 4 Shifting a value by 0 always results in the original value : SELECT bitwise_right_shift ( 20 , 0 ); -- 20 SELECT bitwise_right_shift ( 42 , 0 ); -- 42 Shifting a value by 64 or more bits results in 0 : SELECT bitwise_right_shift ( 12 , 64 ); -- 0 SELECT bitwise_right_shift ( - 45 , 64 ); -- 0 Shifting 0 by a shift always results in 0 : SELECT bitwise_right_shift ( 0 , 1 ); -- 0 SELECT bitwise_right_shift ( 0 , 2 ); -- 0

evidence_span.text: bitwise_right_shift ( value , shift ) → [same as value] #

Returns the logical right shifted value of value . Shifting 8 (binary: 1000 ) by three bits results in 1 (binary: 001 ): SELECT bitwise_right_shift ( 8 , 3 ); -- 1 Shifting 9 (binary: 1001 ) by one bit results in 4 (binary: 100 ): SELECT bitwise_right_shift ( 9 , 1 ); -- 4 Shifting a value by 0 always results in the original value : SELECT bitwise_right_shift ( 20 , 0 ); -- 20 SELECT bitwise_right_shift ( 42 , 0 ); -- 42 Shifting a value by 64 or more bits results in 0 : SELECT bitwise_right_shift ( 12 , 64 ); -- 0 SELECT bitwise_right_shift ( - 45 , 64 ); -- 0 Shifting 0 by a shift always results in 0 : SELECT bitwise_right_shift ( 0 , 1 ); -- 0 SELECT bitwise_right_shift ( 0 , 2 ); -- 0

field_reviews.raw_text: The ALL , ANY and SOME quantifiers can be used together with comparison operators in the following way:
SELECT 'hello' = ANY ( VALUES 'hello' , 'world' ); -- true SELECT 21 < ALL ( VALUES 19 , 20 , 21 ); -- false SELECT 42 >= SOME ( SELECT 41 UNION ALL SELECT 42 UNION ALL SELECT 43 ); -- true
Following are the meanings of some quantifier and comparison operator combinations:
Evaluates to true when A is equal to all values.
Evaluates to true when A doesn’t match any value.
Evaluates to true when A is smaller than the smallest value.
Evaluates to true when A is equal to any of the values. This form is equivalent to A IN (...) .
Evaluates to true when A doesn’t match one or more values.
Evaluates to true when A is smaller than the biggest value.
ANY and SOME have the same meaning and can be used interchangeably.

evidence_span.text: Wrap a SQL value as a JSON scalar value. Supports boolean , all integral and floating-point types, decimal , number , varchar / char , date , time(p) / time(p) with time zone , timestamp(p) / timestamp(p) with time zone . The JSON value keeps the SQL value and type it was built from, except that CHAR values become VARCHAR scalars with their declared padding. Direct casts back to datetime types are supported for DATE and TIME(p) . For TIME WITH TIME ZONE , TIMESTAMP , and TIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONE , use JSON_VALUE with a matching RETURNING type to extract the typed value. JSON text has no datetime type, so serializing a datetime renders the canonical SQL literal as a JSON string. A SQL NULL input yields SQL NULL , not the JSON null value. SELECT json_scalar ( 1 ); -- JSON '1' SELECT json_scalar ( 'abc' ); -- JSON '"abc"' SELECT json_scalar ( CAST ( 'a' AS CHAR ( 3 ))); -- JSON '"a "' SELECT json_scalar ( DATE '2024-01-02' ); -- JSON '"2024-01-02"' SELECT CAST ( json_scalar ( DATE '2024-01-02' ) AS DATE ); -- DATE '2024-01-02' SELECT json_scalar ( CAST ( NULL AS bigint )); -- NULL

evidence_span.text: Returns the source string translated by replacing characters found in the from string with the corresponding characters in the to string. If the from string contains duplicates, only the first is used. If the source character does not exist in the from string, the source character will be copied without translation. If the index of the matching character in the from string is beyond the length of the to string, the source character will be omitted from the resulting string. evidence_span.text: Returns the JSON value deserialized from the input JSON text. This is inverse function to json_format() : SELECT json_parse ( '[1, 2, 3]' ); -- JSON '[1,2,3]' SELECT json_parse ( '"abc"' ); -- JSON '"abc"' Note json_parse() and CAST(string AS JSON) have completely different semantics. json_parse() expects a JSON text conforming to RFC 7159 , and returns the JSON value deserialized from the JSON text. The JSON value can be a JSON object, a JSON array, a JSON string, a JSON number, true , false or null . Character input is UTF-8; a byte-order mark or bytes resembling another encoding do not change that encoding. JSON strings and member names must contain Unicode scalar values, so lone surrogate escapes are rejected. Valid surrogate pairs represent supplementary characters. Exponent-form numbers use DOUBLE semantics. Overflow is rejected, while very small values can underflow to zero. Exact numbers without an exponent retain their precision within the supported numeric representation limits. SELECT json_parse ( 'not_json' ); -- ERROR! SELECT json_parse ( '["a": 1, "b": 2]' ); -- JSON '["a": 1, "b": 2]' SELECT json_parse ( '[1, 2, 3]' ); -- JSON '[1,2,3]' SELECT json_parse ( '"abc"' ); -- JSON '"abc"' SELECT json_parse ( '42' ); -- JSON '42' SELECT json_parse ( 'true' ); -- JSON 'true' SELECT json_parse ( 'null' ); -- JSON 'null' CAST(string AS JSON) takes any VARCHAR value as input, and returns a JSON string with its value set to input string. SELECT CAST ( 'not_json' AS JSON ); -- JSON '"not_json"' SELECT CAST ( '["a": 1, "b": 2]' AS JSON ); -- JSON '"[\"a\": 1, \"b\": 2]"' SELECT CAST ( '[1, 2, 3]' AS JSON ); -- JSON '"[1, 2, 3]"' SELECT CAST ( '"abc"' AS JSON ); -- JSON '"\"abc\""' SELECT CAST ( '42' AS JSON ); -- JSON '"42"' SELECT CAST ( 'true' AS JSON ); -- JSON '"true"' SELECT CAST ( 'null' AS JSON ); -- JSON '"null"'

evidence_span.text: Character input is UTF-8; a byte-order mark or bytes resembling another encoding do not change that encoding. JSON strings and member names must contain Unicode scalar values, so lone surrogate escapes are rejected. Valid surrogate pairs represent supplementary characters.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / Other JSON functions #

evidence_span.text: Exponent-form numbers use DOUBLE semantics. Overflow is rejected, while very small values can underflow to zero. Exact numbers without an exponent retain their precision within the supported numeric representation limits.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / Other JSON functions #

evidence_span.text:
SELECT json_parse('not_json');         -- ERROR!
SELECT json_parse('["a": 1, "b": 2]'); -- JSON '["a": 1, "b": 2]'
SELECT json_parse('[1, 2, 3]');        -- JSON '[1,2,3]'
SELECT json_parse('"abc"');            -- JSON '"abc"'
SELECT json_parse('42');               -- JSON '42'
SELECT json_parse('true');             -- JSON 'true'
SELECT json_parse('null');             -- JSON 'null'

field_reviews.raw_text: The IS [NOT] TRUE , IS [NOT] FALSE , and IS [NOT] UNKNOWN operators test the three-valued result of a boolean expression. Unlike a direct comparison against TRUE or FALSE , these operators always return a non-null boolean, treating a NULL (unknown) operand as a known value. IS UNKNOWN is equivalent to IS NULL on a boolean operand:
SELECT ( 1 > 0 ) IS TRUE ; -- true SELECT ( 1 > 2 ) IS FALSE ; -- true SELECT ( NULL > 0 ) IS UNKNOWN ; -- true SELECT ( NULL > 0 ) IS NOT TRUE ; -- true

WITH text_input(id, text) AS (
         VALUES
             (1, 'The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog'),
             (2, 'The quick and the lazy'),
             (3, 'The quick brown fox jumps over the dog')
     ),
     text_ngrams(id, ngrams) AS (
         SELECT id,
                transform(
                  ngrams(
                    split(text, ' '),
                    4
                  ),
                  token -> array_join(token, ' ')
                )
         FROM text_input
     ),
     minhash_digest(id, digest) AS (
         SELECT id,
                (SELECT make_set_digest(v) FROM unnest(ngrams) u(v))
         FROM text_ngrams
     ),
     setdigest_side_by_side(id1, digest1, id2, digest2) AS (
         SELECT m1.id as id1,
                m1.digest as digest1,
                m2.id as id2,
                m2.digest as digest2
         FROM (SELECT id, digest FROM minhash_digest) m1
         JOIN (SELECT id, digest FROM minhash_digest) m2
           ON m1.id != m2.id AND m1.id < m2.id
     )
SELECT id1,
       id2,
       intersection_cardinality(digest1, digest2) AS intersection_cardinality,
       jaccard_index(digest1, digest2)            AS jaccard_index
FROM setdigest_side_by_side
ORDER BY id1, id2;

evidence_span.text: Trino implements HyperLogLog data sketches as a set of 32-bit buckets which store a maximum hash . They can be stored sparsely (as a map from bucket ID to bucket), or densely (as a contiguous memory block). The HyperLogLog data structure starts as the sparse representation, switching to dense when it is more efficient. The P4HyperLogLog structure is initialized densely and remains dense for its lifetime.

evidence_span.text: The json_value function extracts a scalar SQL value from a JSON value.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_value #

evidence_span.text:
JSON_VALUE(
    json_input [ FORMAT JSON [ ENCODING { UTF8 | UTF16 | UTF32 } ] ],
    json_path
    [ PASSING json_argument [, ...] ]
    [ RETURNING type ]
    [ { ERROR | NULL | DEFAULT expression } ON EMPTY ]
    [ { ERROR | NULL | DEFAULT expression } ON ERROR ]
    )

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_value #

evidence_span.text: The json_path is evaluated using the json_input as the context variable ( $ ), and the passed arguments as the named variables ( $variable_name ).

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_value #

evidence_span.text: The returned value is the SQL scalar returned by the path. By default, it is converted to string ( varchar ). In the RETURNING clause, you can specify other desired type: a character string type, numeric, boolean or datetime type.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_value #

evidence_span.text: json_input is a JSON value, a character string, or a binary string. A string should contain a single JSON item; for a binary string, you can specify encoding.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_value #

evidence_span.text: json_path is a string literal, containing the path mode specification, and the path expression, following the syntax rules described in JSON path syntax and semantics .

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_value #

evidence_span.text:
'strict $.price + $tax'
'lax $[last].abs().floor()'

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_value #

evidence_span.text: In the PASSING clause you can pass arbitrary expressions to be used by the path expression.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_value #

evidence_span.text: PASSING orders.tax AS O_TAX

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_value #

evidence_span.text: The passed parameters can be referenced in the path expression by named variables, prefixed with $ .

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_value #

evidence_span.text: 'strict $[last].price + $O_TAX'

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_value #

evidence_span.text: Additionally to SQL values, you can pass JSON values, specifying the format and optional encoding:

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_value #

evidence_span.text:
PASSING orders.json_desc FORMAT JSON AS o_desc,
        orders.binary_record FORMAT JSON ENCODING UTF16 AS o_rec

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_value #

evidence_span.text: Note that the JSON path language is case-sensitive, while the unquoted SQL identifiers are upper-cased. Therefore, it is recommended to use quoted identifiers in the PASSING clause:

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_value #

evidence_span.text:
'lax $.keyvalue()?(@.name == $KeyName).value' PASSING nation.name AS KeyName --> ERROR; no passed value found
'lax $.keyvalue()?(@.name == $KeyName).value' PASSING nation.name AS "KeyName" --> correct

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_value #

evidence_span.text: If the path returns an empty sequence, the ON EMPTY clause is applied. The default value returned ON EMPTY is NULL . You can also specify the default value:

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_value #

evidence_span.text: DEFAULT -1 ON EMPTY

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_value #

evidence_span.text: If an error occurs, the returned value depends on the ON ERROR clause. The default value returned ON ERROR is NULL . One example of error is multiple items returned by the path. Other errors caught and handled according to the ON ERROR clause are:

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_value #

evidence_span.text: Input conversion errors, such as malformed JSON

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_value #

evidence_span.text: JSON path evaluation errors, e.g. division by zero

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_value #

evidence_span.text: Returned scalar not convertible to the desired type

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_value #

evidence_span.text: The DEFAULT expression in ON EMPTY and ON ERROR is only evaluated when the corresponding branch is taken. If evaluation of the ON EMPTY default itself raises a data exception, the failure cascades to the ON ERROR clause. Subqueries are not supported in DEFAULT expressions.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_value #

evidence_span.text: Examples #

supporting_evidence.section_heading: JSON functions and operators # / json_value #

evidence_span.text: Let customers be a table containing two columns: id:bigint , description:varchar .

If the geometry is a collection of geometries (e.g., GEOMETRYCOLLECTION or MULTI*), returns the geometry at a given index. If the given index is less than 1 or greater than the total number of elements in the collection, returns NULL . Use ST_NumGeometries() to find out the total number of elements. Singular geometries (e.g., POINT, LINESTRING, POLYGON), are treated as collections of one element. Empty geometries are treated as empty collections.

evidence_span.text: Returns string with the substring beginning at position start (1-based, must be greater than 0 ) replaced by replacement . The number of characters removed defaults to the length of replacement . The result keeps the same length as string only when the replaced range lies entirely within string ; when the range extends past the end, the result is longer. For example, overlay('abc' PLACING 'XYZ' FROM 3) returns abXYZ .

evidence_span.text: Returns an arbitrary non-null value x , if one exists. x can be any valid expression. This allows you to return values from columns that are not directly part of the aggregation, including expressions using these columns, in a query. For example, the following query returns the customer name from the name column, and returns the sum of all total prices as customer spend. The aggregation however uses the rows grouped by the customer identifier custkey a required, since only that column is guaranteed to be unique: SELECT sum ( o . totalprice ) as spend , any_value ( c . name ) FROM tpch . tiny . orders o JOIN tpch . tiny . customer c ON o . custkey = c . custkey GROUP BY c . custkey ; ORDER BY spend ;

evidence_span.text: Range operator: BETWEEN #
The BETWEEN operator tests if a value is within a specified range. It uses the syntax value BETWEEN min AND max :

supporting_evidence.section_heading: Comparison functions and operators # / Range operator: BETWEEN #

evidence_span.text: SELECT 3 BETWEEN 2 AND 6;

supporting_evidence.section_heading: Comparison functions and operators # / Range operator: BETWEEN #

evidence_span.text: The preceding statement is equivalent to the following statement:

supporting_evidence.section_heading: Comparison functions and operators # / Range operator: BETWEEN #

evidence_span.text: SELECT 3 >= 2 AND 3 <= 6;

supporting_evidence.section_heading: Comparison functions and operators # / Range operator: BETWEEN #

evidence_span.text: To test if a value does not fall within the specified range use NOT BETWEEN :

supporting_evidence.section_heading: Comparison functions and operators # / Range operator: BETWEEN #

evidence_span.text: SELECT 3 NOT BETWEEN 2 AND 6;

supporting_evidence.section_heading: Comparison functions and operators # / Range operator: BETWEEN #

evidence_span.text: The statement shown above is equivalent to the following statement:

supporting_evidence.section_heading: Comparison functions and operators # / Range operator: BETWEEN #

evidence_span.text: SELECT 3 < 2 OR 3 > 6;

supporting_evidence.section_heading: Comparison functions and operators # / Range operator: BETWEEN #

evidence_span.text: A NULL in a BETWEEN or NOT BETWEEN statement is evaluated using the standard NULL evaluation rules applied to the equivalent expression above:

supporting_evidence.section_heading: Comparison functions and operators # / Range operator: BETWEEN #

evidence_span.text:
SELECT NULL BETWEEN 2 AND 4; -- null

SELECT 2 BETWEEN NULL AND 6; -- null

SELECT 2 BETWEEN 3 AND NULL; -- false

SELECT 8 BETWEEN NULL AND 6; -- false

supporting_evidence.section_heading: Comparison functions and operators # / Range operator: BETWEEN #

evidence_span.text: The BETWEEN and NOT BETWEEN operators can also be used to evaluate any orderable type. For example, a VARCHAR :

supporting_evidence.section_heading: Comparison functions and operators # / Range operator: BETWEEN #

evidence_span.text: SELECT 'Paul' BETWEEN 'John' AND 'Ringo'; -- true

supporting_evidence.section_heading: Comparison functions and operators # / Range operator: BETWEEN #

evidence_span.text: Note that the value, min, and max parameters to BETWEEN and NOT BETWEEN must be the same type. For example, Trino produces an error if you ask it if John is between 2.3 and 35.2 .

supporting_evidence.section_heading: Comparison functions and operators # / Range operator: BETWEEN #

evidence_span.text: Symmetric and asymmetric ranges #

supporting_evidence.section_heading: Comparison functions and operators # / Range operator: BETWEEN #

evidence_span.text: By default the bounds are interpreted in order, so value BETWEEN min AND max only matches when min <= max . This default can be made explicit with ASYMMETRIC :

supporting_evidence.section_heading: Comparison functions and operators # / Range operator: BETWEEN # / Symmetric and asymmetric ranges #

evidence_span.text:
SELECT 3 BETWEEN ASYMMETRIC 2 AND 6; -- true
SELECT 3 BETWEEN ASYMMETRIC 6 AND 2; -- false

supporting_evidence.section_heading: Comparison functions and operators # / Range operator: BETWEEN # / Symmetric and asymmetric ranges #

evidence_span.text: With SYMMETRIC , the two bounds are treated as an unordered pair, so the test succeeds when the value lies between them in either order. value BETWEEN SYMMETRIC min AND max is equivalent to value BETWEEN ASYMMETRIC min AND max OR value BETWEEN ASYMMETRIC max AND min :

supporting_evidence.section_heading: Comparison functions and operators # / Range operator: BETWEEN # / Symmetric and asymmetric ranges #

evidence_span.text:
SELECT 3 BETWEEN SYMMETRIC 2 AND 6; -- true
SELECT 3 BETWEEN SYMMETRIC 6 AND 2; -- true

supporting_evidence.section_heading: Comparison functions and operators # / Range operator: BETWEEN # / Symmetric and asymmetric ranges #

evidence_span.text: SYMMETRIC can be combined with NOT , and follows the same NULL evaluation rules as the equivalent expanded expression.

The IN operator can be used in a WHERE clause to compare column values with a list of values. The list of values can be supplied by a subquery or directly as static values in an array:

supporting_evidence.section_heading: Comparison functions and operators # / Row comparison: IN #

evidence_span.text:
... WHERE column [NOT] IN ('value1','value2');
... WHERE column [NOT] IN ( subquery );

supporting_evidence.section_heading: Comparison functions and operators # / Row comparison: IN #

evidence_span.text: Use the optional NOT keyword to negate the condition.

supporting_evidence.section_heading: Comparison functions and operators # / Row comparison: IN #

evidence_span.text: The following example shows a simple usage with a static array:

supporting_evidence.section_heading: Comparison functions and operators # / Row comparison: IN #

evidence_span.text: SELECT * FROM region WHERE name IN ('AMERICA', 'EUROPE');

supporting_evidence.section_heading: Comparison functions and operators # / Row comparison: IN #

evidence_span.text: The values in the clause are used for multiple comparisons that are combined as a logical OR . The preceding query is equivalent to the following query:

supporting_evidence.section_heading: Comparison functions and operators # / Row comparison: IN #

evidence_span.text: SELECT * FROM region WHERE name = 'AMERICA' OR name = 'EUROPE';

supporting_evidence.section_heading: Comparison functions and operators # / Row comparison: IN #

evidence_span.text: You can negate the comparisons by adding NOT , and get all other regions except the values in list:

supporting_evidence.section_heading: Comparison functions and operators # / Row comparison: IN #

evidence_span.text: SELECT * FROM region WHERE name NOT IN ('AMERICA', 'EUROPE');

supporting_evidence.section_heading: Comparison functions and operators # / Row comparison: IN #

evidence_span.text: When using a subquery to determine the values to use in the comparison, the subquery must return a single column and one or more rows. For example, the following query returns nation name of countries in regions starting with the letter A , specifically Africa, America, and Asia:

supporting_evidence.section_heading: Comparison functions and operators # / Row comparison: IN #

evidence_span.text:
SELECT nation.name
FROM nation
WHERE regionkey IN (
  SELECT regionkey
  FROM region
  WHERE starts_with(name, 'A')
)
ORDER by nation.name;

evidence_span.text: Computes the top frequent values up to buckets elements approximately. Approximate estimation of the function enables us to pick up the frequent values with less memory. Larger capacity improves the accuracy of underlying algorithm with sacrificing the memory capacity. The returned value is a map containing the top elements with corresponding estimated frequency. The error of the function depends on the permutation of the values and its cardinality. We can set the capacity same as the cardinality of the underlying data to achieve the least error. buckets and capacity must be bigint . value can be numeric or string type. The function uses the stream summary data structure proposed in the paper Efficient Computation of Frequent and Top-k Elements in Data Streams by A. Metwalley, D. Agrawl and A. Abbadi.

field_reviews.raw_text: The IS [NOT] TRUE , IS [NOT] FALSE , and IS [NOT] UNKNOWN operators test the three-valued result of a boolean expression. Unlike a direct comparison against TRUE or FALSE , these operators always return a non-null boolean, treating a NULL (unknown) operand as a known value. IS UNKNOWN is equivalent to IS NULL on a boolean operand:
SELECT ( 1 > 0 ) IS TRUE ; -- true SELECT ( 1 > 2 ) IS FALSE ; -- true SELECT ( NULL > 0 ) IS UNKNOWN ; -- true SELECT ( NULL > 0 ) IS NOT TRUE ; -- true

evidence_span.text: IS TRUE, IS FALSE, and IS UNKNOWN #

The IS [NOT] TRUE , IS [NOT] FALSE , and IS [NOT] UNKNOWN operators test the three-valued result of a boolean expression. Unlike a direct comparison against TRUE or FALSE , these operators always return a non-null boolean, treating a NULL (unknown) operand as a known value. IS UNKNOWN is equivalent to IS NULL on a boolean operand:

SELECT (NULL > 0) IS UNKNOWN; -- true

field_reviews.raw_text: The IS [NOT] TRUE , IS [NOT] FALSE , and IS [NOT] UNKNOWN operators test the three-valued result of a boolean expression. Unlike a direct comparison against TRUE or FALSE , these operators always return a non-null boolean, treating a NULL (unknown) operand as a known value. IS UNKNOWN is equivalent to IS NULL on a boolean operand:
SELECT ( 1 > 0 ) IS TRUE ; -- true SELECT ( 1 > 2 ) IS FALSE ; -- true SELECT ( NULL > 0 ) IS UNKNOWN ; -- true SELECT ( NULL > 0 ) IS NOT TRUE ; -- true

evidence_span.text: Converts a Geometry object to a SphericalGeography object on the sphere of the Earth’s radius. This function is only applicable to POINT , MULTIPOINT , LINESTRING , MULTILINESTRING , POLYGON , MULTIPOLYGON geometries defined in 2D space, or GEOMETRYCOLLECTION of such geometries. For each point of the input geometry, it verifies that point.x is within [-180.0, 180.0] and point.y is within [-90.0, 90.0] , and uses them as (longitude, latitude) degrees to construct the shape of the SphericalGeography result. SRID and Z metadata are not part of the SphericalGeography value.
